articles.title: Bryce James' Full Box Score, Highlights From MCBB Debut in Arizona's Upset Loss to UCLA
articles.summary: NBA legend LeBron James' youngest son, Bryce James, made his college basketball debut Monday night for the fifth-ranked Arizona Wildcats.
articles.body:
NBA legend LeBron James' youngest son, Bryce James, made his college basketball debut Monday night for the fifth-ranked Arizona Wildcats.

While James got the start for Arizona, he played only six minutes and did not record a point in the Wildcats' 84-75 upset loss to the No. 22 UCLA Bruins as part of the Hall of Fame Series in Las Vegas.

The 19-year-old James' full stat line from Monday's defeat was as follows:

After redshirting last season as a freshman, James was part of Arizona's starting five on Monday, and he got off to a hot start by dishing out the assist on the Wildcats' first basket of the campaign by Ivan Kharchenkov:

Bryce is looking to follow in the footsteps of his famous father and brother, both of whom are in the NBA.

LeBron, who signed with the Philadelphia 76ers this past offseason, is the NBA's all-time leading scorer and widely regarded as one of the greatest players of all time.

Bryce's older brother, Bronny James, is in the midst of his third season with the Los Angeles Lakers.

Despite putting up subpar numbers in his only collegiate season at USC, Bronny was taken by the Lakers in the second round of the 2024 NBA draft, and he made history by playing alongside his father for two seasons.

Bryce has taken a more deliberate approach than Bronny did by sitting and learning during his first college season before making his debut at the start of the 2026-27 campaign.

It was not an ideal start to the season for James or the Wildcats as a whole, but they figure to settle in with easier games against Cal Poly and Northern Arizona on tap.

articles.title: Knicks' Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart Discuss Pressure of NBA Title Defense Amid Slow Start
articles.summary: New York Knicks stars Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart each acknowledged the pressure of defending their 2026 NBA title in recent interviews with ESPN's Vincent Goodwill.
articles.body:
New York Knicks stars Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart each acknowledged the pressure of defending their 2026 NBA title in recent interviews with ESPN's Vincent Goodwill .

After opening the season with three straight losses, the Knicks have won three of their last four games in a 3-4 start that included two losses to LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers.

"We're in New York. Everything rides on the next game," Hart told Goodwill. "We go on a 10-game winning streak and the next game we lose, they're ready to burn the place down. We know what it is. It's the tough part of being in New York."

Towns said, per Goodwill: "At the end of the day, people knew, when LeBron and the big three were there, you had to go out there and beat them. Everyone brings their best against the New York Knicks. You've got to protect the jersey, the city at all costs."

The Knicks most recently got off to a slow start Monday night against the Brooklyn Nets before heating up in the fourth quarter to extend an intracity winning streak dating back to 2023.

Hart acknowledged after the loss the Knicks were still dealing with their early-season "issues" despite ultimately pulling off the win over the Nets.

He also indicated, not for the first time , he and his teammates are feeling some fatigue after winning a title in mid-June and celebrating over the summer.

"In the summer, obviously you're working out, you're doing that, but then you also enjoy the fruits of the labor of winning in terms of going to brands, going to do appearances... That takes a little bit of a wear on you. And then you get it into it, so sometimes your body has to kind of catch up," Hart told reporters after Monday's win.

The Knicks are currently sitting eighth in the Eastern Conference after their sub-.500 start to the season. The defending champs will look to continue climbing back up the standings starting with a Wednesday night home game against the Chicago Bulls.

articles.title: Kevin Durant Has Tense Exchange With Reporter in Trending Video After Rockets' Win vs. Celtics
articles.summary: Houston Rockets star Kevin Durant didn't want to focus on his individual contributions in Monday's 109-93 win over the Boston Celtics.
articles.body:
Houston Rockets star Kevin Durant didn't want to focus on his individual contributions in Monday's 109-93 win over the Boston Celtics.

The 16-time All-Star had a somewhat muted offensive impact, scoring 12 points on six shots. During the postgame press conference, he and the Houston Chronicle 's Varun Shankar briefly had a pointed back-and-forth about his performance:

Shankar, for his part, pointed out how Monday's game was an exception across Durant's legendary career and part of a larger trend to open the 2026-27 NBA season:

It's easy to understand Durant's perspective and see why he might be irked about focusing on his shot total in a game his team won. At the same time, it's notable when a player of his pedigree is taking a back seat a bit.

KD's scoring average (20.8 points) is on pace to be his lowest since his rookie season in 2007-08. With a full season in Houston under his belt, he and coach Ime Udoka may have found a formula to lighten his workload to the benefit of the entire offense.

The Rockets are second in the league in offensive rating (121.2), per NBA.com , through eight games.

Should this continue, fans won't be looking at Durant's shot figures in a critical light. Instead, the future Hall of Famer will be garnering a lot of praise for transitioning to a slightly lesser role and remaining as efficient as ever.

articles.title: 5-Star SF Malachi Jordan Makes Commitment Decision Between St. John's, Kansas, Vanderbilt
articles.summary: Five-star forward Malachi Jordan will head to the Big Apple for his first year of college.
articles.body:
Five-star forward Malachi Jordan will head to the Big Apple for his first year of college.

Jordan confirmed Tuesday to ESPN's Paul Biancardi and Jeff Borzello he committed to St. John's.

The 6'7" wing is the No. 20 overall player in 247Sports' composite rankings for 2027. Along with the Red Storm, Vanderbilt and Kansas made it to the finalist stage for his signature.

"Coach (Rick) Pitino has a rich history of developing players," Jordan told ESPN. "The only promise he made was that he'd help me reach my full potential. He is true to his word, and I felt like his coaching and character would help get me to the next level."

Since taking the St. John's job, Pitino hasn't hit the recruiting trail particularly hard. The Red Storm were 106th in 247Sports' composite rankings for the 2026 cycle.

Pitino and his staff have focused more on the transfer portal, and the results speak for themselves following back-to-back 30-win seasons.

Jordan's commitment is a sign the Hall of Fame coach hasn't lost his touch on that front.

247Sports director of scouting Adam Finkelstein evaluated the Prolific Prep star in August and called him "one of the most physically gifted prospects in the class."

"For Jordan, it's all about playing in the flow. When he's not trying to do too much, he has enough touch to make open rhythm shots, be a straight-line downhill driver, and even underrated passer," Finkelstein said. "He's also a violent finisher and lob threat whenever he can get to two feet. Conversely though, when he gets caught up in trying to prove himself, or isn't utilized correctly, he gets inefficient. So, it's not so much about his ability to see or make the right play, but more about a willingness to do it."

Jordan is the first recruit in the Red Storm's 2027 class. On his own, he gives Pitino a solid foundation before the coach turns to the portal after the season.

articles.title: LeBron James Sounds Off on Early-Season Injuries in NBA, Points to Pace of Play, Shortened Preseason
articles.summary: Amid a slew of early-season injuries across the NBA, Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has a theory about what is causing some of the league's top stars to go down.
articles.body:
Amid a slew of early-season injuries across the NBA, Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has a theory about what is causing some of the league's top stars to go down.

During this week's episode of the Mind the Game podcast (4:15 mark), James and co-host Steve Nash discussed the season-ending injury suffered by Oklahoma City Thunder star Jalen Williams and other ailing stars like Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring) and Minnesota Timberwolves guard Anthony Edwards (knee). The 41-year-old suggested that players are having trouble transitioning from the offseason to the high pace of regular-season play.

"We go back to the pace of the game right now, and I think that has a lot to do with it," James said. "There's no way that you can simulate the way we're playing in today's game to offseason training. You can do as much as you can, but to jump right into full throttle of how we're playing the game today, I think, is very challenging."

James also pointed to the shortened preseason as a likely factor in these early-season injuries, and he called out performance-based analytics for these recent trends.

"But also, too, I know we hated it as players when we're in it, but the shortening of the preseason could be it as well," he said. "There's really not many two-a-days anymore. The amount of performance teams that's telling guys to not play as much actually might be a little bit more detrimental to our players."

In his 24th NBA season, James is doing everything he can to stay healthy and has played in six out of Philadelphia's eight games. But at this point, it wouldn't surprise anyone if he or anyone else had to miss time this year.

articles.title: Stephen Curry made $2.5 million from $11 million San Francisco property sale after abandoning headquarters plans
articles.summary: Stephen Curry has found an unexpected financial upside in a business project that never made it off the ground.
articles.body: Stephen Curry has found an unexpected financial upside in a business project that never made it off the ground. The Golden State Warriors superstar has sold his San Francisco property for $11 million, nearly two years after purchasing it for $8.5 million. The deal gives him a gross price difference of $2.5 million, even though his original vision for the site never became reality. What began as an ambitious plan to create a central hub for his growing business empire ended with an abandoned construction project and a new owner. The sale also raises questions about Curry's changing real estate strategy.Stephen Curry earns a $2.5 million gross gain from San Francisco property saleCurry's latest real estate move centres on a two-storey commercial building at 600 20th Street in the Dogpatch neighbourhood of San Francisco. The basketball star purchased the property in May 2024 for $8.5 million. At the time, the acquisition appeared to be more than another investment for the NBA champion. It was intended to support the next stage of his career beyond basketball.However, the property changed hands before those plans could take shape. According to property records cited by the San Francisco Chronicle, the building sold for $11 million on August 31, 2026. The buyer was listed as Dane Reinsurance Inc., a Utah-based corporation with an office in San Francisco.The difference between Curry's purchase and selling prices amounts to $2.5 million. That is a notable result for a property that never served its intended purpose. Still, the figure represents a gross gain rather than confirmed take-home profit. Taxes, transaction fees, maintenance expenses and other costs could affect the final return.The location also played an important role in the property's appeal. The building sits near the Pier 70 waterfront, at the corner of 20th and Illinois streets. It is also roughly half a mile from Chase Center, where Curry has spent much of his professional career with the Warriors.The buyer's identity adds another interesting detail. Dane Reinsurance appears to be connected to Corgi, a growing artificial intelligence insurance startup. The company's links to the property bring a technology angle to a transaction that began with a basketball star's business ambitions.Stephen Curry's Thirty Ink headquarters project collapses after union disputeThe property was supposed to become the new headquarters of Thirty Ink, the company that oversees Curry's growing collection of business interests. The Warriors star wanted a dedicated space where his ventures could operate under one roof rather than remain spread across different locations.The original proposal was ambitious. Plans called for replacing the existing structure with a five-storey building covering approximately 25,000 square feet. It would have included office space, laboratories, areas for arts-related activities and a ground-floor community and event space. A rooftop deck was also part of the design.One of the more unusual features was a three-bedroom penthouse on the fifth floor. The residence was intended to accommodate visiting business partners and guests. The development was designed to offer more than conventional office space, reflecting the different interests that make up Curry's business portfolio.However, the project ran into trouble over construction labour. Thirty Ink and the North Coast States Carpenters Union failed to reach an agreement over the use of union workers. Curry's company said it had offered to use union labour for 40% of the construction work, but negotiations did not produce an acceptable arrangement.In April 2025, Thirty Ink confirmed that it would no longer move forward with the development. A company spokesperson expressed frustration over the breakdown in negotiations.“Our dream of building a new Thirty Ink HQ at 600 20th Street has been destroyed by the [Nor Cal Carpenters Union]”The union also defended its position. Its spokesperson, Sam Singer, argued that the selected contractor had a history of conflict with organised labour. The disagreement became a major obstacle, despite efforts from local officials to keep the development alive.The cancellation meant Curry had to reconsider what to do with a property that had originally been purchased for a specific business purpose. Selling the building eventually became the next step.Stephen Curry's business empire extends beyond the basketball courtCurry's interest in the Dogpatch property was closely connected to his ambitions outside the NBA. While fans know him for his shooting ability and championship success, the four-time NBA champion has also spent years developing businesses and projects away from basketball.Thirty Ink serves as the umbrella for his off-court ventures. The organisation has been associated with eight businesses and 13 entities, covering areas such as media, athlete management, business development and philanthropy.A dedicated headquarters would have given those operations a shared base. Its proximity to Chase Center also made the location attractive, particularly for someone whose professional and business activities remain closely connected to the Bay Area.The project also had potential significance for the surrounding neighbourhood. Dogpatch has undergone considerable change, with former industrial areas attracting new businesses and development. A major headquarters backed by a high-profile athlete could have added another reason for companies to consider the area.Curry's decision to abandon the project therefore represented more than a change in property plans. It marked a shift in how he intended to organise his business operations in San Francisco.The eventual buyer brings a different kind of ambition to the building. Corgi, the startup linked to Dane Reinsurance, operates in the artificial intelligence insurance sector. Its reported interest in San Francisco reflects the growing connection between technology companies and the city's commercial property market.For Curry, however, the transaction offers a clean exit from a development that had become difficult to complete.Stephen Curry's $29.1 million Atherton sale adds to his real estate changesThe Dogpatch transaction is not the only major property move involving Curry and his wife, Ayesha. The couple have also made significant changes to their residential real estate portfolio, suggesting that their recent activity extends beyond a single commercial investment.Earlier in 2026, the Currys sold their Atherton estate for $29.1 million. The sale attracted attention because the property was located in one of the most expensive residential communities in the United States.The couple had previously sold another Atherton mansion for $32.1 million, five years before the latest transaction. They also parted ways with their luxury Four Seasons residence in downtown San Francisco in 2022.These transactions offer a broader picture of the couple's changing property interests. Over the years, they have owned homes in several Bay Area communities, including Oakland, Orinda, Walnut Creek and Alamo.Ayesha Curry's business interests have also experienced changes. Her restaurant, International Smoke, which she co-owned with chef Michael Mina, closed its San Francisco location in May 2026 after nine years. The restaurant operated at the base of Millennium Tower and faced challenges linked to reduced foot traffic and construction around the building.None of these developments alone establishes a single reason behind the couple's decisions. However, together they show that the Currys have been reassessing several parts of their Bay Area property and business footprint.Their latest commercial property sale also comes as Curry approaches another important stage in his basketball career. He remains under contract with the Warriors through the 2026-27 season, while questions about a potential contract extension continue.Stephen Curry's property sale comes as San Francisco attracts AI businessesCurry's $11 million property sale also highlights an interesting shift in San Francisco's commercial real estate market. The city has faced considerable challenges since the pandemic, with office vacancies remaining high and several businesses reconsidering their physical workspace requirements.However, the technology sector has started creating fresh interest in selected neighbourhoods. Artificial intelligence companies, in particular, have become an important part of the city's commercial property conversation.Dogpatch and Mission Bay have benefited from renewed attention as businesses look for space outside traditional downtown office districts. Their location, development potential and access to the wider technology community make them attractive to certain investors.The building Curry sold is a useful example of that changing demand. A property that once carried the promise of becoming a basketball superstar's business headquarters has now moved into the hands of a company connected to the AI insurance industry.Commercial broker Charlie McCabe highlighted the renewed appeal of the city while discussing the changing investment climate.“San Francisco stands out for its technology again inventing the future and also for its many real estate opportunities,” he said. “Consequently, new buyers are entering the local market to take financial advantage of our real estate renaissance.”That shift does not mean the city's commercial property market has fully recovered. Challenges remain, and demand is not evenly spread across every neighbourhood or type of building. Still, transactions like Curry's suggest that some investors see fresh opportunities in locations that once struggled to attract buyers.For the Warriors star, the outcome is straightforward. His original development plans did not survive the labour dispute, but the property found another buyer at a higher price. The $2.5 million gross difference gives him a positive result from an investment that failed to deliver its intended business purpose.Curry may have lost the opportunity to build his planned headquarters in Dogpatch, but he has closed that chapter with a sizeable property sale.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Who should lead Liberty next? Familiar faces, rising stars among five candidates
articles.summary: Chris DeMarco has been dismissed. Who will be the next head coach of the New York Liberty? From Kristi Toliver to Kelly Graves, consider these names.
articles.body:
For the third consecutive season, the New York Liberty will have a different head coach.

The Liberty have fired Chris DeMarco after one season on the job . New York won the Commissioner's Cup and swept the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx in the opening round of the playoffs, then lost to the Atlanta Dream in the semifinals. The Liberty finished the season with a 26-18 record.

DeMarco, 40, previously spent 14 seasons with the NBA's Golden State Warriors where he was part of four championship-winning coaching staffs.

Liberty general manager Jonathan Kolb will be making his fourth head coaching hire since getting the job in 2019. He decided not to renew the contract of Katie Smith and hired Walt Hopkins who was dismissed after two seasons. Sandy Brondello was Kolb's next hire, and she led New York to winning the 2024 championship, but was let go after the 2025 season. Kolb then turned to DeMarco, who delivered a mixed bag of results.

The Liberty now need a coach to lead a team with three star players in former league MVPs Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones and four-time all-star Sabrina Ionescu.

Here's a few names to consider as the search begins.

Golden State Valkyries revel in first WNBA championship

After spending 15 years playing in the WNBA, where she was a two-time champion and three time All-Star, the University of Maryland product has spent nearly a decade as an assistant coach in the NBA and WNBA.

Tolliver, 39, worked as an assistant coach with the Washington Wizards and Dallas Mavericks, then became the associate head coach for the Phoenix Mercury under Nate Tibbetts in 2024. She's won everywhere she's been — from winning a national championship with Maryland, to WNBA titles with the Sparks and Mystics, to helping the Mercury make the Finals in 2025.

Over the past few seasons, Tolliver has interviewed for WNBA head coaching gigs. Sooner or later, some team is going to be smart enough to hire her as its head coach.

The Liberty can't undo dismissing Sandy Brondello, but they could hire one of her former assistants. Hodges was on the Liberty bench in 2024 when it won the WNBA championship. Following that season, she joined Rachid Meziane's staff with the Connecticut Sun — now Houston Comets — in an expanded role.

Hodges, 43, is widely seen as a rising star in the coaching ranks. After a lengthy professional playing career that began with the Comets and ended with a club in Spain, she worked two seasons in college basketball as an assistant at Old Dominion and Colgate before being hired by Brondello in New York in 2022. Earlier this season, Hodges filled in for Meziane as head coach for one game and the Sun won, defeating the Mystics.

The New Orleans native was also the head coach of Phantom BC in Unrivaled this past season. Hodges was named Coach of the Year of the professional 3x3 women's basketball league and guided Phantom to an appearance in the championship game.

A Women's Basketball and Naismith Hall of Famer, and one of the greatest WNBA players of all-time, Weatherspoon is a New York Liberty legend. She spent seven of her eight WNBA seasons playing for the Liberty, winning a pair of Defensive Player of the Year awards, earning five all-star nods, leading the league in assists in 1997 and leading the league in steals twice.

The 60-year-old native of Texas and product of Louisiana Tech — where she won an NCAA championship as a player in 1988 — has a long coaching resume, but many would argue she didn't get a fair chance as a WNBA head coach. She was fired after one season leading the Chicago Sky where they went 13-27 in 2024.

Prior to coaching the Sky, Weatherspoon had been the head coach at her alma mater, guiding the Lady Techsters to three NCAA Tournament bids. She was also an assistant coach for the NBA's New Orleans Pelicans and has been a head coach in Unrivaled for the past two seasons.

T-Spoon is widely respected and liked by players around the league. The Liberty could do much worse than giving her another shot at being a head coach in the WNBA.

One of the Liberty's marquee stars, Sabrina Ionescu, is coming off arguably one of her worst years in the WNBA. If her three-game rookie season is removed from the equation, the talented point guard averaged career-lows in assists, rebounds, field goal percentage and 3-point percentage. To get her back on track, why not bring in her college head coach?

Graves has been a college head coach since 1997 and has gone to 15 NCAA Tournaments with three different programs, including a trip to the Final Four in 2019 with an Oregon team powered by Ionescu. Before coming to Oregon, he turned Gonzaga into a mid-major power, advancing to the second weekend of March Madness three times. He's been named conference Coach of the Year 10 times in his career.

If the 63-year-old is tired of dealing with all the changes in college athletics, he could move to the WNBA and simply be a basketball coach and reunite with one of his star players.

The Atlanta Dream and Dallas Wings have found immediate success in hiring coaches from the college ranks who, despite being at mid-major programs, had long track records of success and proved to be winners at every level. Blair-Lewis is someone who fits a similar mold to Jose Fernandez and Karl Smesko.

Blair-Lewis has piled up 415 victories as a college head coach , winning at programs where winning isn't so easy to do. She won a pair of conference championships at Mount St. Mary's, something the program has done just twice since she left in 2007. She then won five conference championships and took Bethune Cookman to the NCAA Tournament for the first time in program history in 2019. Most recently, Blair-Lewis has turned George Mason into a mid-major power, winning 73 games there over the past three seasons and guiding the Patriots to their first-ever March Madness appearance in 2025.

It would be an outside-the-box hire, but it's hard to argue with Blair-Lewis' resume of winning wherever she has been.

articles.title: JuJu Watkins' triumphant return and 3 other takeaways from opening night of the women's college basketball season
articles.summary: All eyes were on Watkins taking the court for the first time since the 2024 NCAA tournament, and she delivered.
articles.body:
The 2026-27 women's college basketball season tipped off Monday with a largely uncompetitive slate of action. The only ranked matchups on the schedule were No. 1 South Carolina and No. 20 Maryland in Paris, and a matchup of No. 12 North Carolina and No. 21 Oklahoma.

South Carolina kept tight hold of its stature as the country's top team by holding off a furious late Maryland comeback in a 101-93 win while Oklahoma's offensive identity showed in a 91-79 win over UNC.

Nine of the the AP top 10 teams in action cracked the century mark: No. 1 South Carolina (101), No. 2 UConn (100), No. 3 USC (100), No. 7 Louisville (119), No. 8 Vanderbilt (112) and No. 9 LSU (129).

All eyes were on JuJu Watkins taking the court for the first time in 588 days after injuring her ACL in the 2025 NCAA tournament. She delivered with 21 points, 5 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals, 1 block and an emotional post-game interview . No. 3 USC defeated UNLV 100-68 in the Hall of Fame Women's Showcase held at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas.

The redshirt senior showed flashes of her typical self in 25 minutes of action, but is still fresh off the injury. Head coach Lindsay Gottlieb said Watkins is on a minutes restriction.

"I think she physically looks great, explosive-wise and all that," Gottlieb said. "It's just finding that rhythm."

Unlike her first two seasons when Watkins scored at least 30 in 22 games, she won't need to take over as regularly as she did for the Trojans to have success.

Sophomore 6-foot-2 guard Jazzy Davidson and freshman 6-3 wing Saniyah Hall, the No. 1 recruit in the class, can help carry the load for a balanced offensive attack. Davidson scored 23 on a standout 10-of-11 shooting from the field, plus 5 rebounds, 4 assists and 2 steals. In her debut, Hall had 22 points while shooting 7-of-8 with 7 rebounds, 1 assist, 2 steals and 2 blocks.

They looked every bit their No. 3 ranking, and worthy of a return as national champion contenders. The Trojans have not made it to a Final Four since 1986.

Maryland gives South Carolina late scare

No. 1 South Carolina turned what was expected to be the day's most closely contested game against No. 20 Maryland into a straight snoozer. The Gamecocks scored 27 fast-break points and 21 points off turnovers in the first half for a 28-point halftime lead. They led by as many as 31 in the third quarter.

But Maryland didn't go quietly in Paris. The Terrapins cut it to nine with 4:30 left, forcing Dawn Staley to call a timeout and reset her group. Maryland cut it to six, 96-90, again in the final minute. The Terps outscored South Carolina, 60-40, in the second half.

Maryland's Addi Mack fueled the comeback with career-best 35 points on 20 field goals, including 6 of 10 from 3-point range. The sophomore guard is one of four returning pieces from a squad that reached the second round of the tournament and will play a key role with senior guard Oluchi Okananwa.

That should be a confidence-booster for Maryland and a solid building block ahead of the Big Ten schedule, where USC and Michigan are top contenders. Maryland will also play No. 2 UConn in the non-conference schedule. The games will help the Terrapins' NCAA tournament resume, and prepare them early to level up.

It's an immediate opportunity for improvement on the South Carolina side that should scare the rest of the country. They played in the previous three championship games, haven't missed a Final Four since 2019 and head coach Dawn Staley schedules these early competitors to make sure those streaks don't end. She called out a lack of "competitive spirit" in the third quarter and described it as a "great learning lesson."

"I thought physically, we probably were a little tired, but when you're physically tired, the mental piece has to kick in," Staley said. "So I don't think we created enough habits when we're tired for us to actually lock in. … We're going to have to figure out how to play a 40-minute game every time we step on the floor, and there are things that we have to challenge them with, with growing and strengthening their mental toughness."

The No. 2 Huskies eased into the schedule with a 100-35 dismantling of Cornell. Sarah Strong, reigning National Player of the Year, and Jovana Popovic, an early contender for Freshman of the Year, each scored an efficient 19. Strong added 4 rebounds, 5 assists and 8 of the team's 25 steals. Twelve players saw at least six minutes of action.

The attention now turns to No. 5 Michigan on Thursday (6:30 p.m. ET, FS1), the first of nine ranked opponents on the boosted non-conference schedule. The Wolverines gave UConn an early scare last November, but the Huskies escaped 72-69 without losing until the Final Four. It's Michigan's season opener, returning their junior core of Syla Swords, Olivia Olson and Mila Holloway.

Buzzer-beater denies resume-boosting win

South Dakota State, a mid-major juggernaut, missed an opportunity at a NCAA tournament resume booster when Creighton guard Ava Zediker's fadeaway jumper bounced in at the buzzer. SDSU lost 73-71.

The Jackrabbits made the previous four NCAA tournaments as Summit League conference tournament champions. But the competition within their league is tighter, and North Dakota State won the regular season title with a shot at an at-large bid. Those don't come around often to non-power conferences.

SDSU's non-conference schedule features No. 6 Texas, No. 22 Oklahoma State, No. 14 Kentucky and No. 19 Ole Miss.

The Jackrabbits are one of the schools testing the NCAA's new age-based eligibility model. They added Mid-Major Player of the Year Brooklyn Meyer to the roster last week for a fifth season after a judge granted a temporary restraining order that allows her to compete while her case is heard. She's a three-time All-Summit League forward and 2026 Summit League tournament MVP.

She would not say when the temporary restraining order expires, according to The Brookings Register . No. 7 Louisville is in a similar predicament with forward Amiya Joyner.

articles.title: LeBron James Says He Tried to Avoid Injury During Jalen Slawson Chase-Down Block in 76ers-Pacers
articles.summary: Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James made a business decision when he was blocked from behind by Indiana Pacers forward Jalen Slawson earlier this season.
articles.body:
Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James made a business decision when he was blocked from behind by Indiana Pacers forward Jalen Slawson earlier this season.

"You're never worried about stepping on somebody when you're younger or if it was multiple bodies in the lane," he said at the 31:57 mark in Tuesday's episode of his Mind the Game podcast.

James said your mindset changes "as you get a little older, or you get a lot older in my case." He cited the Slawson block as an example.

The 22-time All-star was aware of Slawson "hauling ass to get back on defense." Because of that, he settled for a layup instead of a dunk because that minimized the risk of a painful collision.

Chase-down blocks have become a LeBron trademark, but he was on the receiving end of one in Philly's 114-109 win over the Pacers on Oct. 28. On a breakaway in the second quarter, he got his layup attempt swatted away by Slawson.

The refs originally ruled it a foul before overturning the call after a video review.

An NBA player inevitably won't be able to run as fast or jump as high as he gets deeper into his 30s, or 40s in the case of James. The bigger reason the league's highfliers ground their game is that the landings become more painful.

James could've had two or even three points if he gets fouled in the process of throwing down a dunk on Slawson. Leaving that opportunity on the table was worth it avoid potentially costly contact.

articles.title: 'We don't have enough time to recover:' Is the NBA game outpacing the players?
articles.summary: Only two weeks into the season, the NBA has a growing injury problem.
articles.body:
Standing near half-court with a towel draped over his shoulders, Thunder center Isaiah Hartenstein attempted to drum up encouragement for his rookie deputy Aday Mara as he approached the bench. Teammates Micah Peavy and Bennett Stirtz waited to do the same, while occasionally tilting their heads back at the jumbotron, which flashed a deficit of nearly 20 points. Veteran guard Alex Caruso, dressed in street clothes, could only clap his hands in hopes of bringing a jolt of energy that simply would not come in a 119-98 loss to the Rockets — an unimaginable, disheartening new normal.

The 2026-27 season kicked off a fortnight ago, but Oklahoma City has already endured a campaign's worth of misfortune. Jalen Williams, lost to a fractured left fibula and a dislocated ankle . Cason Wallace, lost to a torn left labrum . Chet Holmgren, lost to a right patellar tendon tear . A tight-knit group that has always preached the importance of being where their feet are now is struggling to find its footing. A team that stood atop basketball's pinnacle less than 18 months ago now is dealing with questions about ever seriously challenging again, despite still boasting the reigning MVP and a former Coach of the Year. It's a unique type of hoops purgatory the organization hasn't experienced before.

"The morale's been pretty good all things considered," coach Mark Daigneault said on Saturday. "A week ago, the circumstances were a lot different than they are today. We understand that. We try to have an approach that can transcend these circumstances and the guys have done a great job. Obviously, the challenge is a little different now than it was prior to those injuries, but we have to recalibrate to what the challenge is and attack it a day and a game at a time."

While injuries have always been a part of the game, especially when competing at the highest level of the sport, the widespread volume and degree of ailments is troubling. One team being suddenly down 60% of its projected starting lineup is one thing, albeit a needle-in-a-haystack type probability. But the list of unavailables — Anthony Edwards, Tyrese Haliburton, Ja Morant, Ben Simmons, Jaren Jackson Jr., Paolo Banchero, Jalen Duren, Kawhi Leonard, Jalen Suggs and others — is growing, with various timelines ranging from multiple weeks to multiple months. Stars and teams are also being cautious with back-to-backs, whether due to early load management or having returned from long-term injuries. (The Pacers had 10 players out against the Hawks on Monday night, the second night of a back-to-back, citing a combination of rest and injury management.)

But the games aren't slowing down for anyone. The season has become streamlined to some degree, with the shortening of training camp/preseason (the typical ramp-up period) and the insertion of the NBA Cup. It's clearly taken a toll on the players, which in turn takes a toll on the overall product. And there doesn't seem to be an immediate fix for cramming 82 games into a six-month schedule.

Rockets guard Marcus Smart, who's dealt with serious injuries over his 12-year career, had an honest take on the growing epidemic.

"The level of basketball has become so extreme on the human body and we don't have enough time to recover like we used to," Smart said. "When I first came in the league, training camp and preseason were damn near three weeks, multiple games to get your body ready for an 82-game season. Now, depending on how far you go in the playoffs, you might get two months off? It's tough on the body.

"People don't understand; you're flying, your body's inflamed, you're landing in different time zones, go to sleep late and gotta be up early. Run as hard as you can, jump as high and fast as you can and be as physical as you can. All you're doing is asking yourself for injuries. But we signed up for it, and have to figure out a way to minimize it. Some of our best players are getting hurt and it's very unfortunate. We all want to be out here doing what we love."

There is a long list of sports scientists, doctors, data analysts and professionals who will attempt to dissect such a rapid rise of injuries in a short amount of time. But simply watching every night, the games look more rigorous, more demanding and more taxing.

Possessions are up , with the Chicago Bulls topping out at 110.2 a night, up from 107 courtesy of the 2025-26 Miami Heat. League average pace from the previous campaign is now hovering over the bottom third . The game has also become more aggressive. Last season's Pistons team, thought to be one of the more physical units around, committed 22 fouls per game. That same figure would rank 18th today . More teams are comfortable sending bodies to the offensive glass, with the Milwaukee Bucks' 33 chances per night a whopping 10 marks higher than last season's No. 1. On the defensive end, no team averaged double digits in contested rebound rate last season — there are eight such teams now . Average team speed and distance are up, too.

"There's not just one straightforward answer," said Jeff Stotts, injury analyst and owner of InStreetClothes.com . "I think you're seeing younger players get injured with a higher frequency because they're likely to have more miles on their legs before they get to the NBA. … I think the game has outpaced the player. And now you're asking your bigger, stronger athletes to also cover more ground, not only work on accelerators but also their brakes. Asking our big guys to stretch their games all the way out to the 3-point line. All those things increase the chances and likelihood of injuries occurring along the way."

Last season, only three players averaged more than 36 minutes a night — Amen Thompson, Kevin Durant and Luka Dončić. That list has since nearly tripled in size. The aforementioned list of injured stars sans Haliburton also has another thing in common: all of their usage rates were lower than the previous season. What that means is while you may be on the ball less, you're off the ball more — relocating, cutting, changing direction and using your body in other ways that still can accumulate pressure and load.

A good indicator of injury prevention is measuring an athlete's workload against their overall fitness level. Essentially the more they're asked to do physically, the more time they need to recover.

"We're in this constant back and forth between rest and acute-to-chronic load ratio, where we're trying to minimize spikes," Stotts said. "Sudden increases in load on the body in relationship to the overall conditioning of the athlete. The teams that have found success have found ways to quantify the data in a way that helps buy-in. Some teams won't rest players; others will build it in. There's no great cure."

Is such a spike in absences this early into the season enough to warrant an alternative look at scheduling or the larger umbrella of how the sport is played altogether? No magic wand can guarantee a clean bill of health, but the games, pace and aggression are increasing in frequency — and the players, whom the entire business model and ecosystem revolves around, are suffering because of it.

articles.title: Un Doncic de otro planeta: "Es una supernova, con él vamos en una nave espacial"
articles.standfirst: La NBA se rinde a los pies del genio esloveno, que es venerado por rivales y compañeros: "Cuando él está en cancha vamos a la velocidad de la luz"
articles.summary: La NBA se rinde a los pies del genio esloveno, que es venerado por rivales y compañeros: "Cuando él está en cancha vamos a la velocidad de la luz"
articles.body: Hay jugadores que dominan un partido y otros que hacen que parezca que juegan a otro deporte. Luka Doncic pertenece a estos últimos. Su exhibición ante los Miami Heat, con 42 puntos, 13 asistencias y siete rebotes, fue otro recital de un jugador que ha convertido lo extraordinario en costumbre y que, a sus 27 años, parece no tener techo. La NBA se rinde a sus pies. Lo suyo empieza a escapar de cualquier lógica estadística. Cinco partidos consecutivos anotando al menos 37 puntos, cuatro de ellos superando los 40, y una facilidad insultante para destrozar cualquier defensa que se le ponga por delante. Doncic anota, asiste, rebotea y decide. Lo hace de todas las maneras posibles y con una naturalidad que convierte cada noche en un espectáculo. Ni siquiera los récords parecen estar a su altura. En este arranque de temporada, con los Lakers lanzados (6-2), su candidatura al MVP ya es una realidad. Pero más allá de los números y de las victorias, hay algo que define mejor que nada la dimensión del esloveno: la admiración que despierta entre quienes comparten vestuario con él y, sobre todo, entre quienes sufren sus exhibiciones desde el otro lado de la cancha. Compañeros, rivales y entrenadores se quedan sin calificativos ante un jugador de otro planeta. Porque cuando alguien como Giannis Antetokounmpo, uno de los grandes dominadores de la NBA, asegura que Doncic es "uno de los mejores anotadores que han jugado a este deporte, si no el mejor", sobran las palabras. Su entrenador, JJ Redick, habla de una "supernova"; sus compañeros asisten incrédulos a sus proezas y sus adversarios apenas encuentran respuestas. Luka ya no sólo deslumbra: también provoca reverencia. Él se lo toma como algo normal, como el que va cada día a la oficina y cumple con su trabajo: "Cuando ganamos, la sensación es mucho mejor", dijo el genio esloveno tras su enésimo recital. Y puso en valor la marcha de los angelinos y sus últimos dos triunfos en el crypto.com Arena: "Es fantástico ganar por 20 a un equipo como Miami, es algo realmente increíble, especialmente en noches consecutivas. Pero no soy solo yo, es todo el mundo. Todos están en los lugares correctos y tirando con confianza". Giannis Antetokounmpo, fichaje estrella de los Miami Heat y que sabe por experiencia propia, porque lo ha hecho muchas veces, lo complicado que es firmar guarismos como los de Doncic en la NBA, se descubrió ante la exhibición del exmadridista: "Obviamente, es uno de los mejores anotadores que han jugado a este deporte, si no el mejor. No hablo de ahora. Hablo de todos los tiempos", aseguró. El griego, uno de los atacantes más prolíficos de la NBA desde que debutó con Milwaukee Bucks en la campaña 2013-14 y que cumple su decimocuarta temporada en la Liga, fue el mejor de los Heat con 30 puntos (10/14 t2, 0/3 t3 y 10/15), 12 rebotes, siete asistencias y dos tapones, pero su magnífico partido quedó eclipsado por el ciclón Doncic, a quien rindió pleitesía. "Creo que hay gente que tiene miedo de decirlo, pero Luka tiene que estar entre los mejores anotadores de la historia". En la misma línea apuntó el técnico de Miami Erik Spoelstra: "Es un desafío enorme enfrentarte a un genio como Doncic". JJ Redick, entrenador de los Lakers, no deja de alucinar con las exhibiciones una noche sí y otra también, de la estrella de su equipo, del que destaca su capacidad para hacer monstruosidades como las que logró ante los Heat parezcan fáciles a fuerza de repetirlas una y otra vez. "Es como una supernova, aunque al mismo tiempo parece algo normal", explicó Reddick. "Vivimos en una nave espacial, y vamos a la velocidad de la luz todo el tiempo cuando él está en cancha. Cuando está encendido, es elegir tu veneno, porque puede meter cualquier tiro. Y luego los rivales empiezan a poner a dos sobre el balón, y todos los demás se benefician de eso. Es un motor ofensivo formidable". Sus compañeros, espectadores de excepción que presencian noche tras noche las exhibiciones de Doncic en primera fila o junto a él, tampoco terminan de asimilar la facilidad que tiene para anotar superando incluso las dobles o triples defensas que plantean los rivales sobre él en ocasiones. "Es una locura. Da la sensación de que prácticamente cualquier lanzamiento que realiza, ya sea un tiro de circo, o un triple con un paso atrás normal, o un lanzamiento complicado va a entrar, es como algo irreal", comentó el exterior angelino Quentin Grimes. Y Austin Reaves, su mejor socio en la cancha, ya se queda sin palabras ante las continuas proezas de su gran valedor en los Lakers: "Luka está haciendo cosas increíbles, y cuando él hace eso, simplemente abre la cancha para que todos los demás jueguen sueltos y con confianza". Lo que viene a ser hacer la vida más fácil y mejor a todos cuantos le rodean en su equipo. Normal que tengan en un pedestal al esloveno, al que veneran unánimemente sus compañeros, su público y sus rivales.

articles.title: Caitlin Clark Reveals WNBA's Toughest Player to Defend, Hypes Fever Teammate Kelsey Mitchell
articles.summary: Like a lot of her WNBA peers, Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark does not like to see the ball wind up in the hands of five-time MVP A'ja Wilson.
articles.body:
Like a lot of her WNBA peers, Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark does not like to see the ball wind up in the hands of five-time MVP A'ja Wilson.

Wilson was the first player Clark cited when asked on Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce who are the toughest players in the league to defend.

"I think that would probably be everybody's answer," she said at the 32:47 mark. "She's just so difficult, just her size, her physicality, her athleticism. She can make a mid-range jump shot super consistently. She can stretch the floor when she wants to. And then she can finish around the rim really well."

Clark added that it's often apparent early into a game whether Wilson will basically be unguardable. On those occasions, the focus shifts to limiting the Las Vegas Aces' supporting cast.

Wilson's 22.1-point career scoring average is the highest in WNBA history, and she's tied for the single-game scoring record (53 points).

The 6'4" center operated around the basket and in the mid-range to begin her career and evolved to become an effective stretch 5. She shot above 40 percent from beyond the arc in each of the past two years.

It's not a stretch to say Wilson is on pace to be the WNBA's greatest scorer ever.

Clark went on to remark her Fever teammate Kelsey Mitchell is often near the top of these conversations when she's chatting with players around the WNBA.

Mitchell took her offensive game to another level in 2026. She set career highs in scoring (24.7) and field-goal percentage (50.9). She was third on the MVP ballot and a first-team All-WNBA honoree for the second time.

Next season, Clark may learn the hard way what it's like to defend Mitchell.

The 5'8" guard is headed for free agency and said last month she intends to be a little "selfish" when weighing up her next month. That doesn't guarantee she'll leave Indiana, but the odds have seemingly gone up.

Her exit would be a massive blow to the Fever and make Clark's life more difficult on defense.

articles.title: 76ers' LeBron James Breaks Down Stephen Curry, Kevin Durant Scouting Reports in Video
articles.summary: Alongside Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James, Kevin Durant and Stephen Curry have been the NBA's most dominant forces over the past two decades. Although the three veterans are entering the latter stages of their careers, James hasn't seen much decline in his counterparts.
articles.body:
Alongside Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James, Kevin Durant and Stephen Curry have been the NBA's most dominant forces over the past two decades. Although the three veterans are entering the latter stages of their careers, James hasn't seen much decline in his counterparts.

During the latest episode of the Mind the Game podcast, James offered a scouting report for Durant and Curry (28:05 mark). When co-host Steve Nash asked what has changed about Durant over the years, James offered a succinct response.

James particularly praised Durant for his efficiency. Durant has averaged over 20 points per game every season of his 19-year career. Now in his second season with the Houston Rockets, the 38-year-old is averaging 20.8 points through the first eight games of the season.

"He's so efficient," James said. "He uses his dribble ability and his quick-twitch punches to back the defense up just a little bit just for him to [create space], and they can't get back. I saw one move he had against [San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama] ... He had a double cross against Wemby, shot fake, and Wemby was right there and he just gave a little slight fade and shot it over top of him. ... He's probably the only guy in the league that can probably make that move versus Wemby."

James also marveled at Curry's consistency and noted that the Golden State Warriors sharpshooter remains the most dangerous threat on his team.

"Every time you play Golden State, he's still No. 1 on the scouting report," James said. "No. 1 and No. 2. You have to find him early in transition — with the ball and even more when he's off the ball. If you pick him up too high in the backcourt, then you got to watch for [Warriors forward Draymond Green] because there's going to be a pick in the backcourt, and if the big is not up, he's shooting it."

Although the Warriors started the 2026-27 season with three losses, Curry has led Golden State to five consecutive wins while averaging 30 points per game.

"There's not much that has changed," James added. "You look at his conditioning, he's still in super, ultra condition. If anything, would it be attacks at the rim, maybe, like the rest of us? He's still super efficient, he still shoots the ball better than anybody in the league. The guy seems like he never gets tired. Not much has changed."

While the NBA has changed dramatically over their careers, the three future Hall of Famers are proving they can still make a significant impact for their respective teams. Although they won't be able to outpace Father Time forever, they're hoping to capture at least one more championship before their illustrious careers come to an end.

articles.title: Hazaña histórica del Valencia en casa del campeón Fenerbahce
articles.standfirst: Alexis Peterson abrocha el triunfo taronja con dos tiros libres a un segundo del final (71-73)
articles.summary: Alexis Peterson abrocha el triunfo taronja con dos tiros libres a un segundo del final (71-73)
articles.body: El Valencia Basket venció este martes al Fenerbahce por primera vez en su historia tras diez derrotas seguidas ante el conjunto turco en un partido decidido en los últimos segundos con dos tiros libres de Alexis Peterson, la mejor de las 'taronja' con 21 puntos, que rompieron el empate a 71 con un solo segundo por jugar y que sellaron un triunfo histórico. El Valencia Basket ya avisó y saltó sin complejos a la pista del Fenerbahce y, a base de intensidad defensiva y de acierto exterior respondió, a las primeras canastas recibidas con un parcial de 2-10 que le otorgaba la primera ventaja seria. Los puntos de Alexis Peterson y los triples de Elena Buenavida y de María Araújo obligaban al técnico de las turcas, Ahmet Caki, a buscar una reacción a través de un tiempo muerto (6-13, min.5). El Fenerbahce trató de subir su listón físico y pudo correr aprovechando su balance ofensivo con los puntos de Nell Angloma. Sumando desde el tiro libre, el parcial llegó a ser de 7-0. Pero el Valencia Basket se mantuvo por delante con las acciones individuales de Elizabeth Balogun, Chloe Bibby y Kamila Borkowska. La pívot polaca cerró el cuarto con un 2+1 que frenaba el primer intento de remontada del equipo local (22-23, min.10). El desacierto se apoderó de ambos equipos en los primeros compases del segundo cuarto. Con un contexto de pérdidas y campo abierto, el Fenerbahce se sentía más cómodo pero apenas podía sumar. Solo una canasta lejana de Emma Meesseman parecía activar a su equipo, pero el Valencia Basket se sostenía gracias al acierto y liderazgo de Peterson, que acabaría la primera parte con 11 puntos. Una penetración suya volvía a dejar la distancia en apenas 3 puntos (31-28, min.15). A cada paso que daba el Fenerbahce llegaba la respuesta de un combativo Valencia Basket. Los puntos de Leila Lacan y de Lauren Betts, que se hacía grande en la pintura, eran respondidos por acciones individuales como una bandeja de la canterana Isabel Hernández. Ni siquiera la falta disruptiva señalada en contra de Peterson en los últimos compases de la primera parte desconectó a un conjunto 'taronja' que evitó que el Fenerbahce se fuera al descanso con la máxima diferencia a su favor gracias a una canasta de Borkowska desde el centro de la zona (42-37, min.20). La canasta de la polaca llenó de confianza a un descarado Valencia Basket. De nuevo los triples de Araújo y de Peterson devolvían el control del marcador a un conjunto 'taronja' incisivo y acertado. El Fenerbahce, incómodo, buscó su crecimiento a base de físico e hizo añicos la pintura con los Betts y con las jugadas de tres puntos que provocaron Tima Pouye y Messeeman. Esa superioridad la trasladó a la defensa y con campo abierto, Angloma seguía haciendo daño y obligando al técnico 'taronja', Javi Torralba, a pedir tiempo para tratar de recuperar el control (59-53, min.27). De nuevo con Peterson como principal sustento anotador, el Valencia Basket fue capaz de aguantar con la ausencia de Betts y la diferencia de apenas 5 puntos dejaba todo abierto para el último cuarto. Una falta en ataque de Chloe Bibby terminó con Pouye en el suelo, con la mano en la rodilla y con los gritos de dolor adueñándose del pabellón. La francesa tuvo que abandonar la pista en camilla en un duelo que bajó por completo su temperatura tras la lesión. De nuevo con el partido en marcha, con un parcial de apenas 4-2 en cuatro minutos y con una diferencia de solo 7 puntos, el Valencia Basket continuó creyendo en la victoria y un triple de Balogun y los puntos de Helena Pueyo y Bibby aumentaron la esperanza 'taronja' y la presión para las turcas, que volvían a parar el juego en busca evitar la sorpresa (68-66, min.36). El Fenerbahce, desconectado tras la lesión de Pouye, no encontraba el camino y empezó a perder balones y darle opciones de remontada a un Valencia Basket que necesitó varios ataques para aprovecharlas. Después de los fallos de Raquel Carrera apareció una vez más Peterson para poner por delante de nuevo a su equipo con solo un minuto por jugar. Las de Torralba tenían que defender su único punto de ventaja, que se esfumó en la siguiente acción con los tiros libres de Laura Juskaite (70-69, min.39). Después del tiempo muerto de las valencianas, Bibby fue objeto de falta cuando lanzaba un triple y anotó dos de los tres tiros. De nuevo, un punto de ventaja para defender y de nuevo, otra vez los tiros libres. Esta vez fue Lacan, que también falló uno de los dos tiros. Con todo empatado a 71, la última acción fue para un Valencia Basket que volvió a apoyarse en Peterson. articles.title: Warriors' Draymond Green Reportedly Won't Be Suspended by NBA After Fight With Suns' Dillon Brooks
articles.summary: ESPN's Shams Charania doesn't believe Draymond Green will face additional punishment from the NBA after being ejected from Monday's 116-113 win over the Phoenix Suns in the third quarter after shoving Khaman Maluach to the ground and aggressively grabbing the jersey of Dillon Brooks.
articles.body:
ESPN's Shams Charania doesn't believe Draymond Green will face additional punishment from the NBA after being ejected from Monday's 116-113 win over the Phoenix Suns in the third quarter after shoving Khaman Maluach to the ground and aggressively grabbing the jersey of Dillon Brooks.

"I can report, I do not expect him to have any more discipline on that," Charania said during an appearance on The Pat McAfee Show (8:09 mark). "I don't expect the NBA to discipline Green any further for [the play in question]. So don't expect anything more, but Green clearly got his lick in there."

Green was given a technical after pushing Maluach to the ground and was issued a second technical for his confrontation with Brooks, leading to his ejection. Brooks was also given a technical.

"I was just trying to deescalate the whole thing," Brooks told reporters . "He did a lot there, fell down, and pushed him at the end of it. I was just trying to deescalate it. He was just tweaking all game. So let it be."

The Warriors trailed 67-57 at the time of the ejection but staged a comeback, with Warriors star Stephen Curry suggesting that moment played a role in turning the tide.

"He lit a fire in all of us and we had to respond," he told reporters. "So I'm glad we did. It was a combination of that moment and we got to have our brother's back when he defends us. But it was also this is one of those games, most of the guys are on a back-to-back. Phoenix had been off for a couple days... definitely that moment kept us in the moment."

Head coach Steve Kerr, meanwhile, said the matchup changed tactically after Green got the boot.

"It changed the game for Phoenix because they decided to go small after that," he told reporters. "So it kind of took [forward Oso] Ighodaro out of the game after that. So they played maybe 12 minutes of super small with [forward Ryan] Dunn at the 5. And it kind of opened up the game a little bit. Our crowd got into it and our guys just did a great job of finding energy on a back-to-back."

The Warriors moved to 5-3 on the season with the victory. Were the NBA to suspend Green for a game (or more), he would miss Thursday's home matchup against Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Miami Heat. But it sounds as though his punishment won't extend beyond the 23rd ejection of his career .

articles.body: El Casademont Zaragoza sobrevivió este martes a un final de infarto en Mont-de-Marsan ante el Basket Landes, donde logró una victoria por la mínima (69-70) que le abre las puertas a la segunda fase de la Euroliga, con categoría de invictas, gracias a un sobresaliente partido de Mariona Ortiz, Meritt Hempe y Helena Oma. Hempe, mejpr jugadora del mes de octubre de la Euroliga, empezó a aparecer en la pintura, el Casademont lo pedía, y con ocho puntos dio aire a las mañas, de la mano de Veronika Vorackova que, aunque no anotó, estuvo presente en casi todos los puntos (12-15). Cinco puntos consecutivos de Aleksa Gulbe pusieron el empate en el marcador al inicio del segundo cuarto (17-17) y Mariama Daramy dio la puntilla a un mal parcial de las zaragozanas que, con casi siete minutos por delante, ya estaban en bonus (23-19). A pesar de que las jugadoras zaragozanas no se encontraron cómodas en la cancha francesa, ambientada por una incansable charanga en las gradas, y aunque no anotaron un triple en toda la primera parte, lograron irse al descanso por delante gracias a la segunda unidad con Yarden Garzon, Oma y Nerea Hermosa al frente, y a los pases de Ortiz. (32-34). articles.title: Why isn’t Angel Reese held to the Caitlin Clark standard when fans attack her teammates?
articles.summary: WNBA media demanded Caitlin Clark condemn online trolls for three seasons, but Angel Reese faces silence as her fans target Dream teammates.
articles.body: The WNBA media constantly demands that Caitlin Clark answer for internet trolls. They tell her she needs to condemn "racism, misogyny and homophobia," even though she has nothing to do with the messages other players receive on social media. But does that standard change when the players facing online trolling are being attacked due to their proximity to a different WNBA star, one who receives very different treatment from those same commentators? ANGEL REESE, ATLANTA DREAM DISAPPOINTED AFTER WNBA FINALS GAME 7 LOSS: 'WE'LL BE BACK' Atlanta Dream players Jordin Canada and Rhyne Howard are now on the receiving end. And the hate isn't coming from supposed Caitlin Clark fans; it's coming from supposed Angel Reese fans. Will the commentators who keep assigning Clark responsibility for other people’s behavior apply their standard to Reese? Don't hold your breath. For the record, I don’t think either player owes anyone a statement. Neither Clark nor Reese is responsible for what other people do or say online. However, I do think the people who keep demanding condemnations from Clark owe us an explanation as to why they aren't keeping up that energy when it's Reese at the center. The responsibility assigned to Caitlin Clark The list of WNBA media members who have openly called for Clark to denounce online hate, something Clark has done multiple times by the way, is almost too long to count. But let's recap a few of the biggest ones: Those examples span from 2024 through this season. So, this isn't new. These people have been making demands of Clark for three seasons, despite her repeated condemnations of the behavior. CAITLIN CLARK SAYS SHE BLOCKS SOCIAL MEDIA HATE AND ENJOYS HOSTILE WNBA ROAD CROWDS On July 3, Clark once again delivered a lengthy statement condemning online hate. She explicitly extended that condemnation to the treatment of opponents, teammates and coaches. "The harassment, the hate, none of that is okay. … There should never be question of character. Like I’ve always stood up here and said that and that’s truly what I believe. That’s how I was raised. … none of that is okay. And I don’t want anybody to ever experience that," Clark said. A reporter raised the subject again at her October 8 season-ending news conference. Asked about Kelsey Mitchell’s comments on the treatment she receives, Clark was also asked to address "the attention this team receives because of you, but maybe not attention that you necessarily asked for." There’s that familiar framing again. Other people send the messages, but Clark gets asked to account for the attention surrounding her teammates. So she answered. Again. "As far as people that have used me to demonstrate racist rhetoric or hate or discrimination, that’s not something I stand for," Clark said. The expectations come from commentators, the questions come from reporters, and Clark keeps giving them an answer. But apparently, that still wasn’t enough. On October 23, ESPN analyst Monica McNutt said: "There is no way that someone would use my likeness to support causes that I am against." Clark has already told people she opposes that behavior. Repeatedly. How many more statements would satisfy McNutt? And now that people defending Angel Reese are attacking Reese’s own teammates, does McNutt expect the same response from her? My guess? Not a chance. Where are the calls for Angel Reese to condemn online trolls? Jordin Canada returned to social media after avoiding it during the playoffs and immediately found a reminder of why she had stayed away. "It blows my mind that as fans yall CHOOSE to say the hurtful and cruel things out loud and on here," she wrote, describing the comments as "heartless, rude, insensitive." Some of the posts targeting her and Howard make their allegiance clear. One account accused Howard, coach Karl Smesko and the Dream’s owners of selling Reese out in a supposedly rigged Finals. Another defended Reese while calling Canada and Howard "BOTH selfish players and human beings" and accusing them of not caring about winning. And some of the attacks were explicitly racist, including posts using the N-word. So where is the insistence that Reese address online trolls "invoking her name" as an excuse to attack other players? So far, the WNBA media has been silent. WNBA FINALS TEAMS END SEASON WITH ONE FINAL NATIONAL ANTHEM SNUB AS DREAM, VALKYRIES LEAVE COURT Reese, meanwhile, outlined her plans for the next six months. In an Instagram post (on her private secondary account), Reese announced she is pausing her podcast for the offseason, plans occasional YouTube vlogs and will spend time resting and working out in Florida. Her explanation: "i’m dedicating this off season to myself." Can you imagine Caitlin Clark announcing that she's taking the next six months to focus on herself while her teammates are complaining about receiving nasty messages on social media? The WNBA media might never recover from such a scenario. We’d get days, probably weeks and maybe even months of lectures about leadership, accountability and whether Clark was abandoning the teammates receiving online abuse. Think pieces would be plastered all over The Guardian, The Athletic, ESPN and other left-wing sites explaining how White women have the privilege of focusing on themselves while Black women have no choice but to always worry about everyone else in their "community." They would all demand that Caitlin Clark issue yet another statement. Then, they would complain that the statement wasn’t enough. The whole cycle would fuel the WNBA media ecosystem through the entire offseason. So, where are the lectures for Angel Reese? Anyone see any think pieces about how Reese is being selfish? Didn't think so. The WNBA’s obsession with online trolls All of this unfolds in a league that spends an extraordinary amount of time talking about what people (and bots) say on the internet. In August, after Sophie Cunningham’s comments about "biological men" competing in women’s sports sparked a debate over eligibility, WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told teams an upcoming meeting of the league’s anti-hate task force would address whether males should be eligible to play in the WNBA. Yahoo Sports reported that meeting instead largely focused on online hate directed at players. Even with eligibility rules on the agenda, the WNBA couldn’t stop talking about internet trolls. USA SPORTS, NBC CLAIM RECORD WNBA FINALS RATINGS, BUT COMPARISONS LEAVE OUT IMPORTANT CONTEXT That’s what I wanted to ask Engelbert about when I attended her October 17 press conference before Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. Why does online commentary warrant so much of the league’s time and attention? And does repeatedly highlighting negativity overshadow the positive things happening with attendance and television audiences? I wasn’t called on. Engelbert nevertheless returned to the subject in her final answer, condemning people who sit "behind a keyboard to spew vitriol and hate and racism and misogyny at our players." After all those meetings, statements and lectures, you’d think the reporters, analysts and commentators demanding more from Caitlin Clark would recognize a familiar situation in Atlanta. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Where are you, Elle Duncan, Monica McNutt, Sarah Spain, and Nancy Armour? Where are your demands for Angel Reese to defend her teammates? Again, I don’t think Reese owes anyone a statement. Clark doesn’t, either. But the people who have spent three seasons assigning that responsibility to Clark should explain why their standard apparently disappears when applying it would require them to make demands of Reese. In the WNBA media’s world, Caitlin Clark has to answer for the internet. But Angel Reese gets to focus on herself.

The team said it will give its next update on Leonard's recovery in one week.

Toronto sent Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, a pair of first round draft picks (2031, 2033), a first-round pick swap (2027) and two second-rounders (2030, 2033) to the Los Angeles Clippers for Leonard.

The move was expected to help a young Raptors team take the next step after last season's 46-36 record and playoff berth. Leonard joined a strong core that includes Scottie Barnes, RJ Barrett, Immanuel Quickley, Jakob Poeltl, Collin Murray-Boyles and Ja'Kobe Walter.

articles.title: Valkyries' WNBA Finals Game 7 Win vs. Angel Reese, Dream Makes History with Record TV Viewership
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream made history on Saturday by playing in the first-ever WNBA Finals Game 7, and they made even more history with the audience they drew.
articles.body:
The Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream made history on Saturday by playing in the first-ever WNBA Finals Game 7, and they made even more history with the audience they drew.

The league announced Tuesday that the Valkyries' win over the Dream to clinch their first WNBA title is now the most-watched WNBA playoff game with an average of 3.3 million viewers.

The game is also the second-most-watched WNBA game since 1997.

The millions of viewers who tuned into the game got quite the show.

The game was tied with just over two minutes to play when Gabby Williams gave Golden State the lead with a deep three. The Valkyries then extended the lead to seven heading into the final minute, but Atlanta stayed alive after Allisha Gray made a clutch three to cut the lead to four.

Golden State ultimately managed to ice the game at the line, though, securing its first title in just its second season as a franchise.

Williams led the way for the Valkyries with 30 points, and she took home Finals MVP for her strong performance throughout the series.

The hype around the WNBA continues to get stronger every year, and an exciting finish to the 2026 campaign will only build momentum heading into next season.

articles.title: Luka Doncic Ruling on Technical Foul for Referee Exchange Made By NBA After Lakers' Win vs. Heat
articles.summary: The NBA rescinded the technical foul that Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić received during a recent victory over the Miami Heat, the league announced Tuesday.
articles.body:
The NBA rescinded the technical foul that Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić received during a recent victory over the Miami Heat, the league announced Tuesday.

Dončić was initially given a technical foul in the second quarter of the Lakers' 138-117 win over the Heat on Monday after he appeared to clap in the direction of an official.

He finished with 42 points, 13 assists, seven rebounds and two steals while shooting 14-of-24 from the field in the victory.

Dončić has now scored at least 40 points in four of his seven appearances this season, averaging a league-leading 38.3 points per game.

The six-time All-Star is also recording 8.1 assists, 8.0 rebounds and 1.9 steals per game while connecting on 49.7 percent of his field goals and 42.7 percent of his triples.

Dončić has established himself as one of the NBA's top offensive players throughout his nine years in the association, but he's also developed a reputation for picking up technical fouls by expressing his displeasure with certain calls made by officials.

He amassed 16 technicals during the 2025-26 season, ranking No. 2 among all players. Dončić also racked up 13 technical fouls in just 50 games during his 2024-25 campaign.

After the NBA's decision on Tuesday, the 27-year-old has just one technical to begin the 2026-27 season.

"This season, I'm not trying to get techs," Dončić said on Oct. 21, per ESPN's Anthony Slater .

It would be beneficial for the Lakers if he can avoid reaching 16 technical fouls before the end of the season, as it would result in a one-game suspension. Los Angeles is currently looking to contend in the Western Conference led by Dončić and Austin Reaves following the departure of LeBron James in free agency this summer.

The Lakers hold the No. 4 spot in the West standings with a 6-2 record.

articles.title: J.R. Smith’s arrest uncovers an unexpected LeBron James-Luka Doncic connection after a police officer reveals Lakers frustration

articles.body: Royse City police officers told J.R. Smith they are still mad at LeBron James over the Luka Doncic trade, and they said it just moments before arresting him. Police video obtained by the California Post shows the exchange from a traffic stop in Texas. Officers pulled over the former NBA player because they believed an active warrant existed. One officer, who appeared to be a Dallas Mavericks fan, had a complaint about James.What did the officer say about LeBron James during J.R. Smith’s arrest?Video of J.R. Smith’s Sept. 28 traffic stop in Texas shows officers venting about LeBron James and the Luka Doncic trade right up until a warrant check came back active. Smith was arrested on an assault charge tied to an alleged Sept. 18 incident in Tarrant County, then released. Attorney Justin A. Moore says Smith is presumed innocent. A hearing in the case is still ahead.The stop stayed friendly until the officers asked J.R. Smith about championships. Smith said two, won with the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Los Angeles Lakers. When an officer asked about a ring with Kyrie Irving, Smith answered, “Kyrie and LeBron.”The same officer avoided saying James’s name out loud. Smith asked if the officer was not a fan, and the reply went straight to the February 2025 trade that sent Doncic from Dallas to Los Angeles. “He stole Luka from us,” the officer said. He went on to say Dallas should have let Rick Carlisle coach his own way and work on Doncic’s conditioning. A second officer said nobody on the scene was happy about the deal, and the first officer said again he was still mad.Why did police have a warrant out for Smith?A license plate reader flagged the vehicle of the 41-year-old former guard for an active warrant. The Southlake Police Department wanted Smith on a charge of assault causing bodily injury, family violence, over an alleged Sept. 18 incident in Tarrant County. Once officers confirmed the warrant, the basketball talk ended and Smith was handcuffed.The two-time champion was released a short time later. Attorney Justin A. articles.title: LeBron James’ wife Savannah James candidly admits major lifestyle changes following veteran’s Sixers move that “stress” her out
articles.summary: Savannah James is running a family schedule across three cities.
articles.body: Savannah James is running a family schedule across three cities. After LeBron James left the Lakers for the Philadelphia 76ers, the 40-year-old told the “Baby, This Is Keke Palmer” podcast on Nov. 3 that the planning stresses her out. The 76ers star lives in New York and takes a helicopter to practice in Philadelphia. Savannah stays in Los Angeles with their 12-year-old daughter, while their son Bryce plays college basketball in Arizona. She calls the juggling hard but says the family is handling it, and she feels steadier about it than she once would have.How is Savannah James handling life across three cities?Savannah James says the hardest part is the math of it. LeBron lives in New York, she is in Los Angeles, and the 76ers play in Philadelphia. “The crazy in my life is the fact that I have to figure out how to be three places at once,” Savannah said, adding, “that is crazy. I try not to think about it because it’s gonna stress me out, and I know it has to happen, but that is crazy.”She told Palmer, “I have to figure out how to be three places at once.” She tries not to dwell on it because it stresses her out, but she knows the plan has to work.New York is the family hub. Bronny stays in Los Angeles with the Lakers, and Bryce is in Tucson with the Arizona Wildcats, so even a normal week means checking several calendars. She has already made the trip east.
